publication_type: Topic-level evidence synthesis combining a classroom teacher-perception study, a multi-stakeholder school requirements study, citizen-science school deployment work, a district dashboard case study, and BAS-linked educational-facility monitoring.
country_and_climate: The evidence spans Portugal, Sweden, Romania, the United States, and school-focused frameworks with transfer across climates. This diversity matters because acceptance is shaped not only by the sensing hardware but by school culture, staff workload, privacy expectations, and whether interventions such as window opening or filtration fit local climate and building operation.
objective_and_research_question: The objective is to identify which design choices make classroom monitoring acceptable to teachers, understandable to non-specialists, and easy to integrate into the daily routine of schools. The practical research question is how to turn room-level sensing into a trusted, low-burden support tool rather than an intrusive or confusing extra system for educators and facilities staff.
study_design: The evidence base is mixed-methods. It includes a multi-parameter classroom monitoring campaign paired with teacher perception, stakeholder interviews and student surveys about IoT-assisted wellbeing, citizen-science and proof-of-concept school deployments, district-level operational dashboarding, and building-monitoring studies that combine sensor data with occupant feedback.
educational_context: The strongest directly relevant settings are elementary and secondary school classrooms, with some university classrooms used for prototyping and method development. The shared context is a busy teaching environment where technology must not interrupt instruction, must be understandable without specialist training, and must fit existing roles such as teachers, school administrators, and facilities teams.
sample_and_duration: Key evidence comes from several complementary scales. Canha et al. monitored 9 classrooms across 171 classes in a Portuguese school while collecting teacher perception. Broden et al. gathered qualitative input from 25 staff members and survey responses from 464 students in a Swedish elementary school. Boston Public Schools operated 3,659 classroom sensors across 125 buildings over the 2022-2023 school year, while SchoolAIR combined university-classroom pilot work with a high-school proof of concept.
environmental_variables: For acceptance and usability, the most useful variables are the ones users can understand and act on: true CO2, temperature, relative humidity, PM2.5, and where relevant simple occupancy context, noise, or light. Adding many ambiguous channels can reduce usability because users must then distinguish which traces are direct, which are proxy, and which actually require action.
outdoor_conditions_and_baseline: Outdoor context improves usability because it explains why a recommended action makes sense. A dashboard that says to ventilate without showing that outdoor air is cleaner and thermally tolerable will be harder for staff to trust. Conversely, including baseline context helps schools understand why a room should keep windows closed during smoke, traffic, heat, or cold episodes.
occupancy_and_activity: Integration into school routine depends heavily on schedule and classroom activity. Data are easier for staff to trust when dashboards respect class periods, breaks, teacher-led transitions, and occupancy patterns instead of generating alarms overnight or during vacant periods. This is also why simple timetable integration often improves usability more than adding another sensor channel.
ventilation_and_filtration_operation: Operational acceptance is highest when the monitoring system maps directly to familiar actions such as opening windows, starting a purifier, requesting HVAC inspection, or adjusting room use. Teachers and staff are less likely to use a system that reports abstract indicators without an obvious classroom response or that recommends actions that conflict with comfort, noise control, or lesson flow.
spatial_granularity: Room-level sensing is the right granularity for user acceptance because teachers and facilities staff need to know which actual classroom has a problem. Building-wide averages or generic school scores are too remote from everyday decision-making. At the same time, users usually do not need multiple devices per ordinary classroom unless the room has a known spatial problem.
sensor_specification: The most usable classroom node is unobtrusive, low-noise, clearly labeled, and built around a small number of reliable direct measurements. Sensors that require frequent interaction, display unexplained raw signals, or rely on privacy-sensitive modalities can undermine acceptance even if they are technically interesting. Evidence from classroom and school studies therefore favors a restrained, trustworthy stack over a maximal one.
calibration_and_qaqc: Trust is a usability issue as much as a technical one. Users are unlikely to integrate sensor information into daily decisions if devices seem inconsistent, stale, or unexplained. QA/QC should therefore be visible through simple freshness indicators, clear handling of warm-up and missing data, and documented calibration state so that teachers and staff can distinguish a room problem from a device problem.
acquisition_and_data_quality: Minute-scale collection with smoothed dashboard presentation is a practical compromise for classroom use. The Boston case and adjacent dashboard evidence show that users benefit from stable rolling displays rather than noisy raw traces. Data quality signals such as last update time, offline status, and suspicious-value flags are important usability features because they affect whether staff feel comfortable acting on the dashboard.
sensor_lifecycle: [uncertain] Acceptance declines when systems demand visible maintenance, frequent resets, or recurring unexplained failures. Published school literature discusses trust, privacy, and dashboard clarity more often than detailed lifecycle usability metrics, so the exact relationship between failure patterns and long-term user acceptance is still underreported.
recommended_sensor_by_variable: For daily school usability, prioritize true CO2 for ventilation guidance, direct T/RH for comfort interpretation, and PM2.5 when particle events or filtration decisions matter. Add lux, calibrated acoustic metrics, or direct occupancy only when the school has a clear action path for them and the interface can present them without overwhelming users. This aligns with the acceptance pattern across the literature: a small set of high-value variables is easier to understand and adopt than a crowded multi-signal panel.
useful_output_and_units: The most useful user-facing outputs are CO2 in ppm, temperature in degrees C, RH in percent, PM2.5 in micrograms per cubic meter, status color or severity band, and occupied-time summaries that translate into room-level recommendations. For teachers, short messages such as ventilate now, room recovered, or maintenance review needed are often more usable than long raw tables, provided the raw data remain accessible for technical staff.
direct_measurement_or_proxy: Acceptance improves when the interface clearly distinguishes measured variables from derived judgments. Teachers and school managers should not have to guess whether a value is direct CO2, a PM estimate, a comfort interpretation, or a composite score. Ambiguity here creates distrust and can also make users feel they are being asked to rely on a black box.
measurement_principle_and_selectivity: The principle behind a sensor matters operationally because it affects how confidently staff can interpret it. Direct and selective measurements such as true CO2 or direct T/RH are easier to explain and defend than broad proxy channels such as VOC indexes or inferred occupancy. From a usability perspective, the simpler rule is to expose only those channels whose measurement meaning can be explained in plain language.
useful_range_and_real_performance: A classroom system that saturates, drifts visibly, or behaves erratically during ordinary school conditions quickly loses acceptance. The operational literature therefore favors devices that remain stable across normal occupied classroom conditions and that present smoothed, interpretable values rather than jittery raw feeds. Real performance matters more to usability than nominal laboratory range.
operating_regime: The preferred regime is always-on background monitoring with minimal user intervention. Devices should not require teachers to start sessions manually or interpret frequent setup messages. Data should be captured continuously, summarized appropriately for occupied periods, and surfaced only when staff can do something meaningful with the information.
interferences_and_confounders: Teacher perception, student experience, and measured conditions do not always align, which is itself a major confounder for acceptance. Other recurring confounders are alert fatigue, privacy concern, unclear ownership of response, stale dashboards, room-to-room differences hidden by school averages, and systems that surface too many variables without enough context. A tool can be technically accurate and still be operationally unusable.
affordable_validation_protocol: A practical TCC-level acceptance protocol is to deploy 2 to 5 classroom nodes for several weeks, pair the measurements with short teacher feedback forms, record actual interventions, and interview at least one facilities or school-management stakeholder. Validation should ask not only whether the sensor was accurate enough, but whether users understood the display, trusted the alerts, and could act on them within normal school routines.
validation_metrics: Acceptance-oriented validation should include uptime, dashboard freshness, false-alert frequency, percentage of alerts acknowledged, intervention completion rate, and simple user feedback on clarity, burden, and trust. When possible, compare objective conditions to subjective teacher or occupant perception so the system can be designed around the known gap between measured and perceived quality.
installation_and_enclosure: Usable school devices should be compact, visually neutral, quiet, and mounted where they do not interfere with teaching or cleaning. The enclosure should make the device look intentional rather than improvised, while still allowing correct airflow and sensor function. Highly visible or awkwardly mounted devices can trigger tampering, distraction, or skepticism.
hardware_integration: From a usability standpoint, hardware integration should favor silent operation, stable power, local buffering, and minimal dependence on user interaction. If privacy-sensitive channels are included, processing should stay as local as possible and only the necessary summaries should leave the device. The hardware stack should support a simple end-user experience even if the technical backend is richer.
total_implementation_cost: [uncertain] Acceptance is helped by low per-room cost because affordable systems are easier to scale equitably across schools instead of being limited to showcase rooms. A practical core classroom node still tends to fall in the same broad low-hundreds-or-less U.S. dollar range seen in adjacent syntheses, but for usability the more important cost is often staff time: onboarding, explanation, support, and response. Published acceptance papers rarely provide a full costed usability model.
evidence_maturity: Evidence maturity is strong for two conclusions: school stakeholders want technology that supports wellbeing rather than surveillance, and measured classroom conditions do not always match teacher perception. It is moderate for dashboard and workflow design principles, and lower for long-term formal usability benchmarking across many schools. The field has more descriptive acceptance evidence than standardized human-factors evaluation.
variable_specific_cautions: Do not present the system as if it diagnoses safety or health by itself. Do not equate a composite score with a direct measurement. Avoid raw audio retention and avoid unnecessary people-monitoring features. Acceptance can also fall if schools perceive the system as evaluating teacher behavior instead of room conditions, so governance and framing are part of the technical design.
system_architecture: The most usable architecture is room node plus simple dashboard plus annotation and maintenance path. Teachers need a concise room-status view and practical actions, while facilities staff need diagnostics, history, and room comparison. A system that stops at data collection without a route to explanation or response will be harder to integrate into daily school routine.
connectivity_and_protocols: Reliable connectivity matters to trust, but most users should never need to think about protocol choice. Wi-Fi with MQTT or HTTPS is generally acceptable when it keeps data fresh and support manageable. When connectivity is unreliable, the dashboard should reflect that clearly rather than silently showing stale room values that users may misinterpret as current conditions.
interoperability_and_data_model: Integration into school routine improves when monitoring data can align with schedules, room identifiers, maintenance workflows, and where relevant building controls. Open fields for room ID, timestamp, occupied status, QA flag, and intervention state are usually enough for a TCC-scale system. Interoperability matters here because a tool is easier to adopt when it fits existing school processes instead of requiring a parallel manual workflow.
cybersecurity_privacy_and_ethics: Privacy is a central acceptance issue. Broden et al. explicitly identify significant privacy concerns in school environments, and the broader school-monitoring literature shows that trust drops quickly when users suspect hidden behavior tracking. Ethical deployment therefore requires minimal data collection, clear disclosure, role-based access, and a governance model that emphasizes student and staff wellbeing rather than surveillance or performance monitoring.
analytical_methods: The most useful analytical pattern for acceptance is mixed interpretation: objective time-series plus schedule context plus short user feedback. Rolling averages, occupied-period summaries, room ranking, and simple event annotation are usually more usable than opaque machine-learning outputs. More advanced models can remain in the background, but the visible layer should stay interpretable.
derived_index_or_model: [uncertain] A practical usability model is a room-status traffic light supported by a small number of explanatory variables and an optional annotation field. This kind of derived status can reduce cognitive load for educators, but only if the underlying logic is transparent and the raw measurements remain visible to technical staff. The literature supports this design direction operationally, but there is still limited formal evidence on one best derived usability model for schools.
decision_rules_and_standards: Usable rules are simple, contextual, and role-aware. For teachers, the system should recommend actions that fit the lesson rhythm, such as brief window opening when outdoor conditions permit or notifying facilities for persistent problems. For administrators and facilities teams, persistence-based thresholds and room ranking are more useful than isolated spikes. Acceptance improves when users can see why an alert appeared and what response is expected from them.
intervention_and_automation: The most acceptable intervention pattern is human-centered and supervised. Monitoring should support teachers, students, and facilities staff with prompts, not surprise them with opaque automation. Where automation exists, it should be low risk, easy to override, and clearly communicated so that school users remain confident that the system serves the learning environment rather than controlling it unpredictably.
environmental_outcomes: When accepted and routinely used, classroom monitoring improves observability of stale air, thermal discomfort, particle events, and persistent problem rooms. The main environmental benefit is not the graph itself but the fact that staff can connect measured conditions to ordinary school actions such as ventilation, filtration, maintenance requests, or changes in room use.
health_and_learning_outcomes: [uncertain] The strongest evidence is still indirect. Better acceptance and usability increase the chance that schools will actually respond to poor room conditions, which can support comfort, attention, and wellbeing. However, the literature does not yet establish a strong causal link between monitoring-system usability alone and improved learning or health outcomes independent of the interventions that follow.
objective_subjective_integration: This topic is defined by the need to combine both layers. Canha et al. show that teacher perception does not fully map onto measured classroom conditions, while Broden et al. show that school stakeholders have substantive needs and concerns that must shape IoT design. The best integration model is therefore not sensor-only or survey-only, but objective monitoring complemented by targeted, low-burden subjective feedback.
quantitative_results: Canha et al. monitored 171 classes in 9 classrooms and found that teacher perception did not fully match measured indoor conditions, underscoring the need for interpretable objective monitoring. Broden et al. gathered 25 staff interviews and workshops plus survey data from 464 students, showing multi-stakeholder alignment on many wellbeing requirements while also highlighting privacy concerns. Boston Public Schools demonstrated institutional-scale operational adoption with 3,659 sensors across 125 buildings and 245 million CO2 measurements in one school year. Rus et al. reported strong agreement between fixed KNX sensors and professional instruments, with correlations up to 0.98 for CO2 and RH and up to 0.97 for temperature, while also observing that subjective IAQ feedback could remain mixed.
feasibility_and_acceptance: Acceptance is best when the system is framed as room-quality support, uses a restrained and trustworthy variable set, protects privacy, and maps alerts to concrete school actions. Teachers and students are more likely to engage when the technology is unobtrusive and understandable, while facilities teams are more likely to adopt it when it helps prioritize real problems instead of generating noise. The field increasingly supports participatory, action-oriented deployment rather than purely technical rollout.
validity_and_limitations: Most acceptance evidence still comes from case studies, pilots, and mixed-methods work rather than standardized multi-site usability trials. Cultural context, school governance, age group, and privacy expectations can change acceptance significantly. Findings are therefore robust enough to guide design principles, but less precise for predicting exactly how any one school community will respond before local piloting.
contribution_and_research_gaps: The literature now supports a clear design direction for school acceptance: keep the sensing core understandable, involve stakeholders early, expose freshness and uncertainty, and connect room data to ordinary school actions. The main gaps are longer-term usability studies after novelty wears off, stronger comparison of dashboard designs for different school roles, clearer evidence on how privacy framing changes adoption, and more published studies that measure whether accepted systems remain actively used over multiple school years.
